item.title: How Contractors Got Found Before Google, and Why That Changed
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: For decades a contractor’s reputation traveled by mouth, and that still matters, but the first conversation about you now happens on a phone screen. Word of…
item.content:encoded:
For decades a contractor’s reputation traveled by mouth, and that still matters, but the first conversation about you now happens on a phone screen.

Word of mouth, then

Before the internet, a homeowner who wanted a remodel asked a neighbor, a friend or a relative who they knew. The answer was usually one of two stories: a great contractor worth calling, or a horror story to avoid.

Either way, you were found because someone vouched for you. If you did good work, the same people hired you again and told others. That is still the cheapest and best source of work.

Word of mouth, now

Homeowners still ask friends and neighbors. But the next step has changed: they check the name on their phone.

If a rival has a modern site, a complete Google listing and recent reviews, that rival gets the call even when your work is better. Few people scroll to the second page of search results. A referral that leads to an empty or outdated search result can die right there.

So referrals and search now work as one system. Referrals bring people to your name, and your online presence decides whether they call.

What a customer sees when they search for you

Search your own business name and your trade plus your town, on your phone. Then ask what a stranger would conclude.

  • Is there a Google listing with your correct phone number, hours and service area?
  • Do you have recent reviews, and do you answer them?
  • Does your site load fast on a phone, with a tap-to-call button above the fold?
  • Are there photos of real jobs rather than stock images?
  • Do the first results belong to you, or to directory and lead sites that collect contact details and resell them?

That last point matters. Directory sites often rank above individual contractors, so owning a strong listing and site is how you show up beside or above them.

A good-looking site is not the same as being found

Contractors often say they paid for a professional website and still never appear in search. Looks and visibility are separate jobs. Before paying anyone for SEO, ask what exactly they will change, how they will measure it, and what you can check yourself, such as where you rank for your trade plus your town on a phone, and how many calls come from your Google listing. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain this plainly or who guarantees first-page results.

If referrals have slowed

Many established contractors who ran on referrals for years say calls have dropped over the last decade. People talk less about who they hired and search more. You do not need to abandon word of mouth. You need a findable online presence so the referral has somewhere to land. It is also a good project to hand to a younger family member or a part-time helper.

Checklist, and the last step

  1. Claim your Google listing and fill every field.
  2. Ask each happy customer for a review, and reply to every one.
  3. Make sure your site works well on a phone.
  4. Make sure every call that comes from those places gets answered.

item.title: 5 Mistakes That Keep Handymen Underpaid (and How to Avoid Them)
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Undercharging, weak communication, sloppy books: these five mistakes keep handymen underpaid. See what they are and how to fix each one.
item.content:encoded:
Six and a half years into running his own handyman business, Alan Lee of The Handyman Journey says he made plenty of mistakes, and that many other handymen are making the same ones. If you want to earn more and work fewer late nights, these are the five to watch for.

1. Not charging enough

This is the big one. If you undercharge, you cannot cover your bills, so many new handymen end up quitting and going back to a regular job. Most of us are not in this to do charity work. We are in it for financial freedom and control of our time, and neither is possible when your prices are too low. Charge what the work is worth to the customer, and do quality work so the price holds up.

2. Weak communication

Misunderstandings are common, so err on the side of over-communicating. Rephrase important points two or three different ways until the client clearly understands. Then under-promise and over-deliver. If a job could take three months and you finish in one, you are a hero. If you promised it in one and it takes three, you have a problem. Tell clients about dust, setup, and extra visits ahead of time so nothing catches them off guard.

3. Cutting your price for “future work”

Someone offers you a lot of work later if you give them a deal today. Nine times out of ten, the future work never comes, and you are the one who loses. Quote the first job at the price you need to charge. If you go low now, the client will expect low prices forever, and a reputation as the cheap guy is very hard to shake.

4. Sloppy bookkeeping

Handymen buy materials, truck parts, tools, and gas, and they bring in income. If you do not track both sides, you will not know whether you are making money or how much tax you owe. Alan admits he did not even know his first-year income. Accounting software such as QuickBooks Online, connected to your bank and cards, makes it far easier to see profit and loss.

5. Growing without a plan

Hiring a second technician sounds like the obvious way to make more, but you are still stuck with all the admin: calls, estimates, invoices, work orders, and taxes. Alan chose to grow the admin side first, so he could stop working evenings and weekends. Decide on purpose how you want to grow before you hire.

The takeaway

All five mistakes come back to treating your handyman work as a real business. Price for profit, communicate clearly, hold your prices, track your numbers, and plan your growth. The next two posts go deeper into each of these.

item.title: From Jack of All Trades to Go-To Guy: A Growth Plan for Handymen
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Saying yes to every job keeps handymen stuck. Here’s a six-step plan for picking a niche, finding your ideal customer, and becoming the go-to name in your…
item.content:encoded:
Most handymen stay stuck because they say “yes” to everything. The jobs are random, the pricing is guesswork, and every week starts from zero. The fix is simple: stop being a generalist and build a business around a few services you can do fast, well, and repeat. Here’s how to turn that into a growth plan.

Step 1: Choose your niche on purpose

Look for work that commonly breaks or gets damaged in a house: holes in walls, worn doors and locks, old fixtures. Those problems never stop, and people pay to have them fixed. Choose one or two services, such as drywall plus doors, or fixtures plus fans, and commit to them for a few months.

Step 2: Aim at a specific customer

Working handymen show what this looks like in practice. One focuses on new-build homes, doing builder-grade closet shelving, 8-foot doors, and lights and fans, and plans a business card that simply says “doors, lights, shelves.” Another avoids low-paying, high-competition work such as basic TV mounting and installs slim LED recessed lights instead. A third loves storm door installs where the customer supplies the door, with an upsell on new brick molding. The pattern: a narrow offer, a clear customer, and a bit of competition avoided.

Step 3: Become the known name

The more jobs you do of one type, the more neighbors, realtors, and builders hear that you are the person for it. Ask every happy customer for a Google review and a referral, and keep your marketing message to one line. Specific beats broad: “I fix doors and locks” is easier to remember than “I do all kinds of repairs.”

Step 4: Increase profit per visit

Three levers: (1) let customers supply materials, (2) bundle related services, and (3) suggest things they didn’t think about. A TV mount becomes a TV mount, hidden wires, and a soundbar. A fixture swap becomes a fixture swap plus a fan upgrade. You earn more per trip without finding a new customer.

Step 5: Protect your time and reputation

Watch for jobs that will blow up your schedule, like fixtures with hundreds of crystals, or repairs where a prior leak could get blamed on you. A handyman we know avoids faucets, disposals, and bidets for exactly that reason, so decide your own limits. Also check licensing: some states restrict plumbing and electrical work for handymen, so know your local rules before you sell those services.

Step 6: Keep learning

Learn from other tradespeople and add one new skill at a time. Tips travel fast in this business, so keep your eyes and ears open. Also, let your best-paying service guide what you learn next. It doesn’t make sense to learn how to do something that only earns a couple bucks.

Your 30-day starting plan

Week 1: Pick one or two niches and list the exact tools you need.

Week 2: Practice on friends’ or family’s homes, and time each job.

Week 3: Write a one-line offer and put it on your card, profile, and local groups.

Week 4: Quote your first five paid jobs with one add-on each, and ask each customer for a review.

Specializing is not about limiting your income. It is how you get faster, build trust, and charge more for the same hour of work.

item.title: Why Pay-Per-Lead Sites Cost More Than They Advertise
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: The price on a pay-per-lead invoice is rarely the price of a job. In most cases, you pay when a homeowner fills in a form, even if they are ready to start…
item.content:encoded:
The price on a pay-per-lead invoice is rarely the price of a job. In most cases, you pay when a homeowner fills in a form, even if they are ready to start or other contractors receive it.

One lead may be in many inboxes

In many lead-sale models, one homeowner request is sent to multiple contractors at once. So the moment you pay, you are racing others to a phone the homeowner may not answer.

The homeowner often filled in the form to see options, not to take a bunch of calls from contractors trying to pitch them. That mismatch explains why so many paid leads never pick up, or already have a bid in hand and only want a price check.

Cost per lead is the wrong number

The number that matters is cost per job won: total lead spend divided by jobs booked. Here is an illustrative example:

Plug in your own numbers. If a $40 lead turns into a $480 acquisition cost, the platform’s price tag was never the real price.

What contractors commonly report

Contractors who have bought leads describe a familiar pattern: prices that creep up, homeowners who never answer, leads that already have bids, and homeowners surprised to be called by several companies. Some describe trouble cancelling.

Regulators have also looked at the category. In January 2023 the FTC accepted a settlement with HomeAdvisor over allegations that it overstated how often its leads turned into jobs and misdescribed where some leads came from. The dispute ended in a $7.2 million settlement while the company did not admit wrongdoing (TechCrunch).

Read the terms before you buy

Before spending, ask three questions:

  1. Do you pay for leads that never answer?
  2. Can you cancel without a fee?
  3. Does the contract renew automatically?

Some contractors report being locked into multi-year agreements, or getting leads for the wrong kind of job. Get the answers in writing.

Keep the comparison fair, too. Google’s own Local Services Ads also charge per lead, so the same cost-per-job math applies there. Lead sites are not evil. They just should not be your only source, because you cannot control their price, their lead quality or how your reviews appear.

What to do instead

  1. Work out your cost per job won for every channel, using the table above.
  2. Put effort into channels you own: a clear website, a complete Google listing and steady reviews.
  3. Answer every call that comes in, from any source. A lead you never speak to cost money and returned nothing.

item.title: How Specializing Lets a Handyman Charge More
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: Specialists don’t compete on price. Here’s why getting really good at one or two jobs lets handymen charge more, and how bundling services adds revenue on…
item.content:encoded:
When you are known for one thing, customers stop comparing you against the cheapest person on a TaskRabbit. They are buying certainty. You have done this exact job dozens of times, you show up with the right parts and tools, and you finish quickly. Speed is the part many new handymen miss: the faster you are, the higher the hourly rate you can earn even if the customer pays a fair flat price.

Let the customer bring the materials

A good way to keep your take home rate higher is by making sure the client supplies the necessary product or materials, such as a TV, a faucet, or a smart doorbell. That keeps your costs down and removes the headache of buying, returning, and marking up parts. The profit margin goes up because you are selling labor and skill, not inventory.

Set expectations before you arrive

Certain projects require a lot more time and can put your profit at risk. Decorative light fixtures with endless crystals can eat an afternoon, so agree beforehand who assembles them. And on a garbage disposal install with a dishwasher, knocking out the knockout plug is easy to forget (… trust us, we’ve all done it), so build it into your checklist. Small misses like these cost you a free return visit and a bit of goodwill.

Bundle and offer solutions customers did not know they needed

When someone books a TV mount, ask whether they want the wires hidden in the wall, and whether they would like a soundbar installed at the same time. Customers rarely think about cable runs until the TV is up and the wire is dangling. Solving a problem they did not know they had is where the extra revenue comes from, and it makes the job feel like a better experience.

A reality check before you raise your rates

Treat the hourly numbers as a goal, not a promise, and check your local rules first. Remember, some plumbing and electrical work may be restricted by licensing, so look up what your state or city allows before advertising swaps like faucets, disposals, or light fixtures.

A simple pricing approach

  1. Pick one or two niches from the list in the previous post.
  2. Track how long each job really takes over your first ten jobs.
  3. Quote a flat price based on your fastest reliable time, plus a margin for surprises.
  4. Add an optional add-on to every quote, such as hidden wires or a second fixture.
  5. Raise your price once you are booked out for a few weeks.

item.title: The 5 Most Profitable Handyman Jobs You Can Start Offering Today
item.dc:creator: Bolt Answering Content Team
item.description: If you are still taking every random job that comes your way, you are probably leaving money on the table. The handymen who earn the most tend to pick a…
item.content:encoded:
If you are still taking every random job that comes your way, you are probably leaving money on the table. The handymen who earn the most tend to pick a small set of repeatable jobs, get fast at them, and let their reputation do the marketing. Here are five of the best places to start, counted down from five to one, with tips on what makes each one pay.

5. Drywall repair

Drywall is high skill but needs very little material to get started. Plenty of homeowners cannot fix a hole themselves, and plenty of homes have holes. It is hard at first, but every patch makes you faster, and once you are known as the person who makes walls disappear, referrals follow.

4. Door and lock installation

Replacing doorknobs and deadbolts is simple work that many people would rather not touch. Doors are one of the things in a house that constantly break or get damaged, so demand never dries up. The tool list is short, which keeps your profit margin high, and you can become the go-to door person in your neighborhood.

3. Ceiling fans and light fixtures

Most residential fans and fixtures are close to identical, so each install teaches you something that applies to the next one. One warning: a fixture the customer calls “easy” can turn out to have a thousand tiny parts, and hanging them can take hours. Settle up front who handles these intricate fixtures or price that job differently.

2. Faucets and garbage disposals

The theme here is swapping, not building. Pulling out a kitchen faucet and putting in a new one is far quicker than anything that involves construction. Disposals are similar, since the problem is often a tripped breaker, a clog, or a simple replacement.

1. TV mounting and smart home installs

This category is big enough that some people build whole businesses on it: TVs, soundbars, video doorbells, smart thermostats, and a growing list of connected appliances. The work is cleaner than drywall or plumbing, customers usually buy the equipment, and it feels like a specialist service. Bigger TVs may need a second person, but otherwise the barrier is low.

The common thread

All five jobs are fast to learn, need few tools, are easy to repeat, and often let the customer supply the materials. Pick one or two, get very good at them, and you stop competing as a generalist and start stuffing your pockets.
